Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval containing $0$. For an integer $r\ge1$, $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous. Let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open reference region whose boundary is, near each boundary point and in coordinates $y=Qx+c$ for some $Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ and $c\in\mathbb R^3$ with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$, the graph of a $C^1$ function; let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline B\subset U$. A smooth motion is a map $\chi:I\times U\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ such that, for every $t\in I$, the map $\chi_t(a):=\chi(t,a)$ is a bijection from $U$ onto an open set $\chi_t(U)$ with a $C^2$ inverse and with $\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$ for all $a\in U$. The coordinate $a$ labels a reference point and $x=\chi(t,a)$ is its current position; $\Omega:=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$ is the swept open set and $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$ is the current image of $B$.

For $(t,x)\in\Omega$, define the inverse label $A(t,x)$ by $\chi(t,A(t,x))=x$, and put $F(t,a):=D_a\chi(t,a)$ and $J(t,a):=\det F(t,a)$. The joint map $H(t,a):=(t,\chi(t,a))$ is injective and has block-triangular derivative with determinant $J(t,a)>0$. The Euclidean inverse function theorem therefore gives local $C^1$ inverses; they agree on overlaps because the label is unique, so $A$ is globally $C^1$ on $\Omega$. Define the Eulerian velocity field $u(t,x):=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$; an Eulerian field is a function of time and current position. Thus $u$ is $C^1$.

For any $C^1$ scalar or vector field $f$ on $\Omega$, its material derivative is $D_tf:=\partial_tf+(D_xf)u$, componentwise; it is the derivative along the curves $t\mapsto\chi(t,a)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$.
The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every regular chart density is continuous and strictly positive. The chart integral on a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface defines a finite Borel measure independent of the finite charts and subordinate partitions. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ its density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. On a one-sided domain boundary the outward unit normal agrees on chart overlaps and is continuous.

Here $C^r$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through total order $r$ exist and are continuous; a diffeomorphism is a bijection with an inverse of the stated regularity. Write $A(t,x)=\chi_t^{-1}(x)$, $u(t,x)=\partial_t\chi(t,A(t,x))$, $F=D_a\chi$, $L=D_xu$, and $\theta=\operatorname{tr}L=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$. Here $D_a\chi$ and $D_xu$ are matrices of coordinate partial derivatives. The joint inverse $A$ has domain $\Omega=\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(U)\}$.

A compact Jordan set $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ means a compact set whose boundary, for every $\varepsilon>0$, is coverable by finitely many axis-parallel boxes with total volume less than $\varepsilon$, where a box's volume is the product of its side lengths. Integrals over such sets are Riemann integrals, defined by extending the integrand by zero to a containing rectangle. Let $K\subset U$ be any compact Jordan set and let $q,\rho\in C^1(\Omega,\mathbb R)$. Then $A$ is jointly $C^2$, and for every $a\in U$ and $t\in I$,

$$\partial_tF(t,a)=L(t,\chi(t,a))F(t,a),\qquad \partial_tJ(t,a)=J(t,a)\theta(t,\chi(t,a)),\qquad J(t,a)=J(0,a)\exp\!\left(\int_0^t\theta(s,\chi(s,a))\,ds\right).$$

For every $t\in I$, change of variables and material transport satisfy

$$\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_Kq(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)\,da,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(K)}q(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(D_tq(t,x)+q(t,x)\theta(t,x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\bigl(\partial_tq+\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)\bigr)\,dx,$$

where $D_tq=\partial_tq+u\cdot\nabla_xq$ and $\nabla_x\!\cdot(qu)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}(qu_i)$. Define $M_K(t):=\int_{\chi_t(K)}\rho(t,x)\,dx$. This is a mathematical equivalence; it adopts no physical mass-conservation postulate and asserts no weak-field or vacuum extension.

Adopt the Axiom of Countable Choice, meaning that every sequence of nonempty sets admits a choice function. For $n\ge1$, use the complete Euclidean Lebesgue measure space $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal L_n,\lambda_n)$, where $\mathcal L_n=\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Caratheodory-measurable family for Lebesgue outer measure and $\lambda_n$ is that outer measure restricted to $\mathcal L_n$. The sigma-algebra and complete-measure assertions are the Lebesgue measure theorem under this axiom. For a Lebesgue-measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, use the trace sigma-algebra $\mathcal L_E:=\{E\cap B:B\in\mathcal L_n\}$ and the measure $\lambda_E(A):=\lambda_n(A)$ for $A\in\mathcal L_E$; its countable additivity is inherited from $\lambda_n$. A map $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal L_E$ for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, where the Borel sigma-algebra is generated by the open sets. For matrix-valued maps use their finite coordinate arrays. A property holds almost everywhere on $E$ when its exceptional set is contained in a measurable $\lambda_E$-null set. Nonnegative integrals are suprema of nonnegative simple minorants; signed real integrals are the difference of the positive- and negative-part integrals when those parts are finite. Finite-dimensional integrals are taken componentwise.

Let $T>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $m\ge1$ be an integer. Put $D:=\Omega\times[0,T)\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ in spatial-first coordinates $(x,t)$. Both $D$ and $\Omega$ are Borel and hence Lebesgue measurable. Spatial integrals use $\lambda_\Omega$ from $\lambda_3$, and space-time integrals use $\lambda_D$ from $\lambda_4$. For a finite coordinate array $v$, set $\|v\|_1:=\sum_i|v_i|$, summing all entries for a matrix. A measurable field $f:E\to\mathbb R^k$ is locally integrable when $\int_K\|f\|_1\,d\lambda_E<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq E$. For $E=D$ the compact sets are taken in the relative topology, including those meeting $t=0$. Fields on $D$ are identified up to $\lambda_D$-almost-everywhere equality, and initial fields on $\Omega$ up to $\lambda_\Omega$-almost-everywhere equality. The slice $\Omega\times\{0\}$ is contained in a Lebesgue-null coordinate hyperplane in $\mathbb R^4$; values of a space-time representative on that slice do not determine the separately prescribed initial field.

In the displayed weak identities, $\int_0^T\int_\Omega f\,dx\,dt$ denotes the joint integral of the zero extension of $f$ from $D$ with respect to $\lambda_4$. For each test, its compact support bounds the test and its first derivatives, so every component of the tested products is measurable and is bounded in absolute value by a fixed multiple of the norm of a locally integrable field on that compact set. Thus all tested products and their finite sums have finite signed integrals. Euclidean Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ is the completed product of $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_1$; completed-product Fubini therefore also gives the displayed iterated notation, with section integrals taken for almost every time and set to zero on a measurable exceptional null set. No integrability of every individual time slice is required. The integral is unchanged by the stated almost-everywhere identifications. The same conventions apply to the scalar inequality and to the initial integrals on $\Omega$.

Let $U: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$, $F: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^{m\times3}$, and $S: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^m$ be such fields, and let $U_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be locally integrable. For each row $a$, define $(\operatorname{div}_x F)_a=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}F_{aj}$ in the distributional sense, and define $F:\nabla_x\phi=\sum_{a=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^3F_{aj}\partial_{x_j}\phi_a$. The equation $\partial_tU+\operatorname{div}_xF=S$ with distributional initial datum $U_0$ means that for every $\phi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T);\mathbb R^m)$, continuously differentiable up to $t=0$ and supported away from $\partial\Omega$ and $t=T$,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega U_0(x)\cdot\phi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$

No boundary condition on $\partial\Omega$ is encoded because the test fields are supported away from it. This initial identity specifies the initial datum distributionally; it does not assert $U(\cdot,t)\to U_0$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ or any other stronger trace topology. Such a trace must be assumed or proved separately. The fields are abstract mathematical variables; no physical unit system or balance postulate is imposed.

For locally integrable scalar fields $H,R:D\to\mathbb R$ and $H_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a locally integrable flux $Q: \Omega\times[0,T)\to\mathbb R^3$, the inequality $\partial_tH+\operatorname{div}_x Q\ge R$ with initial datum $H_0$ means that for every nonnegative $\psi\in C_c^1(\Omega\times[0,T))$ with the same support convention,

$$\int_0^T\!\int_\Omega\bigl(H\,\partial_t\psi+Q\cdot\nabla_x\psi+R\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega H_0(x)\psi(x,0)\,dx\le0.$$

derivations.claim: By [A2] and [F2], $P$ and $P^{-1}$ preserve the Lebesgue sigma-algebra and measure. Pullback by $P$ bijects nonnegative simple minorants and preserves their level-set measures, so the nonnegative integral is preserved by its defining supremum; applying positive and negative parts gives the same conclusion for the integrable tested scalar products in [F1]. Thus the time-first coordinates and the spatial-first weak definition give the same test integrals. For a test $\phi$ supported in $\mathcal O$, apply the product rule to the space-time current $(U^\pm,F_1^\pm,F_2^\pm,F_3^\pm)$ separately on $\mathcal O^-$ and $\mathcal O^+$. Coordinatewise integration by parts in $t,x_1,x_2,x_3$ gives $\int_{\mathcal O}(U\cdot\partial_t\phi+F:\nabla_x\phi+S\cdot\phi)=-\int_{\mathcal O^-}W^-\cdot\phi-\int_{\mathcal O^+}W^+\cdot\phi-\int_{J\times D}K_{\rm graph}\cdot\phi(t,x',h(t,x'))\,dx'\,dt$, where $W^\pm=\partial_tU^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xF^\pm-S^\pm$ and $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]$. Compact support removes all outer-boundary terms; the remaining graph term is the difference of the two side conormal fluxes.

The unnormalised space-time conormal from minus to plus is $(-\partial_th,-\nabla_{x'}h,1)$. Its contraction with the jump current equals $K_{\rm graph}=[F_3]-\partial_th[U]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[F_{1,2}]=\lambda([F]n-V_n[U])$. Since $\lambda>0$, the graph coefficient vanishes exactly when $[F]n-V_n[U]=0$, and has the same sign as the scalar entropy jump coefficient.

If the weak identity holds, choose tests supported wholly inside either side in step 1.1. Each continuous component of $W^\pm$ must vanish: a nonzero value would have a fixed strict sign on a small ball and contradict the identity for a nonnegative $C^1$ bump there. With these bulk terms zero, step 1.1 gives zero integral of $K_{\rm graph}$ against every trace of a test. Any compactly supported $C^1$ graph test $\zeta(t,x')$ extends to the patch as $\phi(t,x',x_3)=\zeta(t,x')\eta(x_3-h(t,x'))$, where $\eta$ is a $C^1$ cutoff with $\eta(0)=1$ and sufficiently small support. Such a uniform tube lies in $\mathcal O$ because the graph over $\operatorname{supp}\zeta$ is compact in this open patch. A nonzero component of continuous $K_{\rm graph}$ would have a fixed sign on a small graph patch and contradict the identity. Hence $W^\pm=0$ and $K_{\rm graph}=0$. Conversely, these equalities make the weak integral zero by step 1.1, and step 1.2 gives the stated jump condition.

For the scalar inequality, step 1.1 gives the weak integral as the negative of the bulk integrals of $g^\pm=\partial_tH^\pm+\operatorname{div}_xG^\pm-R^\pm$ and the negative graph integral with coefficient $K_H=[G_3]-\partial_th[H]-\nabla_{x'}h\cdot[G_{1,2}]$. If both bulk residuals and $K_H$ are nonnegative, the weak integral is nonpositive for every nonnegative test. Conversely, a negative bulk residual at a point admits a nonnegative bump supported on that side and violates the weak inequality. If $K_H<0$ at a graph point, continuity gives a smaller graph patch where $K_H$ is bounded above by a negative constant. Choose a nonnegative test with fixed positive trace on that patch and support in a tube of width $\varepsilon$ about the graph. The negative interface contribution to the weak integral is positive and independent of $\varepsilon$, while the bounded bulk terms have magnitude $O(\varepsilon)$; for small enough $\varepsilon$ the weak integral is positive, a contradiction. Hence both the side inequalities and $K_H\ge0$ are necessary. Step 1.2 shows $K_H=\lambda([G]\cdot n-V_n[H])$, so the stated jump sign is equivalent.
